title: Agentic Architecture
goal: Understand how an AI agent works: a loop that calls a model, runs tools, and repeats until done.

steps.title: An agent is a while loop, not a program
steps.inshort: An AI agent keeps calling the model, doing whatever it asks, and calling again — until the model says it's done.
steps.lead: Think of it like this: you send a message to the AI, it replies. If it needs a tool (like reading a file or running code), it asks. You do that, then send the result back. The AI replies again. This back-and-forth cycle is the agent.
points: Every message must include the full conversation history — the AI doesn't remember anything between calls
A response has content blocks (text, tool requests) and a stop_reason field
When the AI wants a tool, it sends a tool_use block — you run the tool and send back a tool_result
Each tool_result must match the tool_use_id from the request
steps.code:
while True:
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=M, messages=messages, tools=tools
    )
    messages.append({"role": "assistant",
        "content": response.content})
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = [run_tool(b) for b in response.content
        if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user",
        "content": results})
steps.takeaway: The AI asks, your code decides. stop_reason is the switch.

steps.title: One field decides when to stop
steps.inshort: stop_reason == tool_use means keep going. stop_reason == end_turn means done. That's it.
steps.lead: Two values do all the work. When the model wants a tool, stop_reason is tool_use — keep looping. When it's finished, stop_reason is end_turn — stop and give the answer.
points: tool_use: the model wants a tool, keep looping
end_turn: the model is finished, exit the loop
max_tokens and stop_sequence are also stopping signals to handle
refusal means the model declined — not the same as success
steps.caption: The loop your code controls. It only continues while stop_reason says tool_use.
steps.takeaway: Read the field, not the prose. If it's not tool_use, you're done.

steps.title: Don't check the text to know when to stop
steps.inshort: Looking for words like 'done' or 'finished' in the response to decide when to stop the loop.
steps.lead: It feels natural and works in early testing. But it's the most fragile choice you can make.
points: Natural language is ambiguous — the model might explain its reasoning without actually calling a tool
Wording changes across prompts and model versions — a match that works today breaks tomorrow
The structured signal never changes: a tool request always has stop_reason: tool_use
steps.why: Checking the text fails both ways: it stops too early when the model is explaining, and runs forever when the model is working silently.
steps.takeaway: Text is for humans. stop_reason is for code.

steps.title: Don't use a fixed iteration count to stop
steps.inshort: Running exactly N iterations and returning whatever you have, instead of checking if the AI is actually done.
steps.lead: A cap on iterations is a good safety net. But using it as the main way to decide the work is done is a mistake.
points: If your loop runs exactly 5 times, you might cut off useful work
The cap doesn't know if the AI is actually finished
The correct design uses stop_reason to decide completion, with a generous cap as backup
steps.takeaway: Caps are safety nets. stop_reason is the decision.

steps.title: Don't stop just because text appeared
steps.inshort: If the assistant returned a text block, thinking the work is finished.
steps.lead: This breaks because the AI often sends a text block AND a tool request in the same response — explaining what it's about to do while also asking for a tool.
points: If you see text and think the work is done, you return half-finished output and never run the tool
The text describes what the model wants to do — not whether it's finished
Only stop_reason tells you definitively what comes next
steps.takeaway: Text narrates what's happening. stop_reason decides what happens next.

steps.title: The one signal that matters
steps.inshort: Every other approach uses a proxy. Only stop_reason is the real answer.
steps.lead: The correct loop reads stop_reason and branches on it. Continue while tool_use, stop on end_turn. The cap is just a backup, never the main logic.
points: Checking text → trusts wording → unreliable
Counting iterations → trusts a counter → can cut off work
Checking content shape → trusts block type → can stop early
Reading stop_reason → trusts the API's structured signal → always correct
steps.takeaway: Structured signal over prose. One authoritative field over three guesses.

steps.title: Quick check — do you understand?
steps.inshort: What's wrong with checking if the response contains text to know when to stop?
steps.lead: The AI can send text AND a tool request at the same time. If you stop on text, you miss the tool call and get half-finished results.
steps.takeaway: The fix is always: read stop_reason.

steps.title: What matters most
steps.inshort: Here are the key takeaways for this domain.
points: stop_reason is the only authoritative signal for loop control
Text, counters, and content checks are all proxies — unreliable
A generous iteration cap is fine as a safety net
The loop continues while tool_use, stops on end_turn
steps.takeaway: Your loop is driven by one field: stop_reason. Everything else is a trap.
steps.lead: This is the summary of everything you just learned. Keep these points handy.
